requested.title: Canonicalised out-dir turns a symlink in the project into a recursive delete outside it
`--out-dir` recursively force-deletes any directory it names, including the project root
Freshly minted MOCHI_KEY written to .env with default world-readable permissions
Non-global KEY_LINE regex rewrites only the first MOCHI_KEY line, so rotation can silently not take effect
Agent-instruction file written from an unauthenticated, env-overridable URL with the review gate skipped on first write
svelteConfigPath is unreachable from the build CLI, so production artifacts can be compiled with the wrong Svelte config
Agent-name allowlist in resolveTarget is bypassed by prototype-chain keys
Extraction's process-global Bun.plugin and captured state are never scoped or cleared, leaking a stub `mochi-framework` namespace into the live dev server
Virtual module's `default` export exposes the unproxied `Mochi`, bypassing the capturing serve() stub

rawResponses.rawText:
I have verified every finding statically, with two benign library-behaviour probes (Bun's default file mode, Bun's env parser, and Bun's `rmSync` symlink semantics) to settle causal claims. Here are my verdicts.

  {
    "findingId": "F1",
    "verdict": "true-positive",
    "adjustedSeverity": "MEDIUM",
    "reasoning": "Mechanism fully confirmed. `resolveOutDir` (compiler/resolveOutDir.ts) canonicalises via `realpathSync`, returning the *target* of a leaf symlink; build.ts L105 feeds that into the unguarded `rmSync(outDir, { recursive: true, force: true })` at L112 with no containment, lstat or build-marker check anywhere in the path (I read `checkEnvironment()` and cli.ts — nothing validates the out-dir). I verified the causal attribution empirically rather than assuming it: `fs.rmSync(<dirSymlink>, {recursive:true, force:true})` under Bun 1.4.5 unlinks the link and leaves the target fully intact, so without canonicalisation this really is harmless, and commit 0f4dadb6 (#366, 'canonicalise the out-dir so a symlinked path doesn't break island resolution') is what converted a link-unlink into a recursive delete of the target. The dangling-symlink carve-out is also right: `realpathSync` throws ENOENT, the loop reconstructs the uncanonicalised `<proj>/.mochi`, and only the link dies. Reachability holds: `.mochi` is the default out-dir, git checks out a tracked symlink regardless of `.gitignore` (the repo ignores `.mochi`, but `git add -f` makes it tracked and checkout materialises it), and a production build reaches L112 with `outDir === baseOutDir`. I agree with the finding's own honesty about the ceiling — `extractServeOptions` imports the entry first, so a code-capable adversary already has execution, and the residual value is against write-but-not-code adversaries (shared CI workspaces) and against code review, where a symlink is a one-line diff. The Mochi.ts:600 comparison is also correct: it is `development`-gated and targets the nested `<outDir>/dev`, whose leaf is not canonicalised. MEDIUM is the right band. Overlaps F2 at the same line but is a distinct issue: different trigger (attacker-planted symlink vs. operator-named path), different threat actor, and a different fix (containment + lstat refusal does not stop `--out-dir .`, which is inside the root).",

    "findingId": "F2",
    "verdict": "true-positive",

So: the defect is real and the docblock's stated invariant ('replacing `Mochi.serve` with a stub') is genuinely broken, but there is no scenario in which a working project is harmed. The one-line fix in the recommendation — build the exports object once and point `default` at the same proxied shape — is worth taking for the invariant alone.",

**Summary:** all nine findings hold up as described; none were fixed in current `HEAD` (latest commit `1cb3f3ce`) and none are duplicates. Three empirical checks mattered to the verdicts rather than just confirming prose:

- **F1's causal attribution is exactly right** — I confirmed Bun's `rmSync(symlink, {recursive, force})` unlinks the link and leaves the target intact, so `resolveOutDir`'s canonicalisation (added in #366) is precisely what converts a harmless link-unlink into a recursive delete outside the project.
- **F4's severity claim holds** — Bun's env parser lets the *last* duplicate `MOCHI_KEY=` win, so replacing only the first genuinely leaves the live secret unrotated while reporting success. Its secondary `export MOCHI_KEY=` sub-case is weaker than written (the appended line wins, so that path doesn't silently fail); I noted that in the verdict.
- **F9 is strictly latent** — Bun hard-errors on a default import of a default-less ESM module, so no working app can reach the unproxied `Mochi`.

Two notes where I departed from the findings' own framing: **F8 understates its reach** (the `packages: 'external'` entry bundle means the whole hot-swapped app graph sees the stub namespace after the first dev rebuild, not just lazy chunks), and I kept **F1 and F2 separate** despite sharing line 112 — different trigger, different actor, and a containment check that fixes F1 does nothing for `--out-dir .`.

I confirmed the bin is `src/cli/cli.js` with `#!/usr/bin/env bun`, and Bun's documented env loading reads `.env`, then `.env.{production,development,test}` by NODE_ENV, then `.env.local` from the cwd — and this repo's own `.gitignore` ignores `.env`, `.env.local` and the `*.local` variants but *not* `.env.development`/`.env.production`, which is exactly the committed-env-file gap described. `http://` is accepted. (3) L73-77 check only `res.ok`, then `res.text()` is written verbatim at L89 — no digest, signature, content-type or size check, and `fetch` follows redirects, so the final responder controls the instructions. The mitigation I weighed against this: anyone who can commit `.env.development` can usually commit `.claude/skills/mochi/SKILL.md` or `CLAUDE.md` directly, so the env-redirect adds little for a repo-write adversary. What survives that argument is the part needing no repo access at all — a compromise of mochi.fast, its DNS or a redirect hop installs agent instructions into every project that runs the command, with zero prompt on first write and a diff the operator may rubber-stamp afterwards. That is a genuine supply-chain weakness on a path the project's own threat model already lists, and MEDIUM is the right band for prompt injection into a tool-holding agent.

Verified end to end. `svelteConfigPath` is a real, documented serve option (types.ts L608-612; docs/160-serve-options.md L74; docs/165-svelte-config.md L37-44 says explicitly 'Pass `svelteConfigPath` to `Mochi.serve()` or `build()` to load the config from somewhere else'), and `build()` accepts it (build.ts L38-39) and consumes it at L146. The CLI bridges neither half: `parseArgs` (cli.ts L139-149) declares `entry`, `out-dir`, `public-dir`, `asset-prefix`, `minifier`, `dev`, `force` and nothing else, and the `build({...})` call (L219-236) forwards markdown, svelteCompiler, optimize, minifier, barrelWarnings, fonts, errorPage, resources, protection, publicDir and assetPrefix — but not `svelteConfigPath`. A repo-wide grep for the identifier confirms the only consumers are types.ts, build.ts and Mochi.ts:580; nothing in cli.ts touches it. So `build()` always calls `loadSvelteConfig(undefined)`, which resolves `path.resolve('svelte.config.js')` from the cwd (svelteConfig.ts L22). The divergence claim is correct too: `Mochi.serve()` honours the option at Mochi.ts:580, and production with a prebuilt manifest takes the `fromManifest` branch (Mochi.ts L562-566) and never recompiles, so `compilerOptions` such as `css`, `customElement`, `warningFilter` or runes settings apply in dev and silently do not in prod. The CLI's own `--help` ('The build reads its config straight from the entry's `Mochi.serve()` call, so the prebuilt manifest stays single-sourced with the runtime') makes the omission a contract violation rather than an undocumented gap. Correctly rated a bug rather than a security issue, since `loadSvelteConfig` logs 'No Svelte config found at … — using framework defaults' (L24), making the mismatch noisy. The recommendation's parenthetical about `outDir` being deliberately unmirrored is also accurate.

Confirmed by reading resolveTarget (cli.ts L66-71). `SKILL_TARGETS` is `Object.keys(SKILL_DESTS)`, so the `includes` check fails for prototype keys, and the fallback `TARGET_ALIASES[name] ?? null` on a plain object literal walks `Object.prototype`: `__proto__` yields `Object.prototype`, `constructor` yields the `Object` function, `toString`/`valueOf`/`hasOwnProperty` yield functions — all truthy, all passing `if (!target)` at L76, all handed to `updateSkill({ target })`. I then traced the consequence precisely: `SKILL_DESTS[target]` coerces the key to a string (`'[object Object]'`, `'function Object() { [native code] }'`), misses, and `path.resolve(cwd, undefined)` at updateSkill.ts L78 throws `TypeError [ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE]`, which `runUpdateSkill`'s catch (cli.ts L108-112) prints and exits 1 on. I checked whether any `Object.prototype` key could stringify into a usable `SKILL_DESTS` key — none can — so there is no path traversal and no write to an unintended destination; the impact really is confined to error-message quality. One ordering detail the finding omits: `updateSkill` fetches (L67) *before* computing `dest` (L78), so with `MOCHI_SKILL_URL` unset and the live mochi.fast URL still 404ing (per cli.test.ts's own comment), the HTTP-404 error usually fires first and the TypeError is only reached when the fetch succeeds. Either way the user gets an internal error instead of the intended '[mochi] Unknown agent: … Valid agents: …' message, and cli.test.ts only exercises `'bogus'`, so the hole is uncovered. Worth fixing as validation hygiene exactly as described — `Object.hasOwn` or `Object.create(null)`/`Map` — since the same pattern elsewhere, where the resolved value *is* a usable key, would be a real allowlist bypass.

Every structural claim verified, and reachability is in fact broader than the finding allows. The plugin is latched by `pluginRegistrationDone` (L35/L78) and `Bun.plugin` offers no deregistration, so `build.module('mochi-framework', …)` hijacks that exact specifier for the process lifetime. devWatcher.ts L342 does call `extractServeOptions(outFile, { fresh: true })` from inside a live server, and L314-325 builds the entry with `packages: 'external'`, which leaves `mochi-framework` as a bare runtime specifier in `entry.js` — so from the first rebuild onward the hot-swapped entry graph resolves through the virtual module and sees a frozen `isBuilding: true` (L72) plus `Mochi` as the capturing proxy, while framework internals keep reading the real `isBuildingEntry()` through the relative import (I confirmed buildFlag.ts is only consumed by queue.ts and extractServeOptions; `isBuilding` is a public export at index.ts L59, so app code guarding side effects on it would misbehave in dev after a rebuild). That is a wider blast radius than the 'lazily-loaded chunks and freshImportBundled' framing, not a narrower one, and the rest of the reachability analysis is right: compiled Svelte externalises only `svelte`/`svelte/*` (ComponentRegistry.ts L906) with `mochi-env` shadowing the specifier, so SSR output never emits a bare import. The `captured` claim is also correct — it is nulled only at L81 on entry and never after `return captured` (L98), so it stays non-null between calls and a `Mochi.serve()` reached through the leaked proxy outside an extraction would throw the misleading 'called more than once' error from L49-51. I confirmed the non-security framing: `startDevWatcher` is reached only under `if (development)` (Mochi.ts L2151-2152), so the plugin never lands in a production server, and the L65 spread keeps every other export real. The suggested fix (an `extracting` flag consulted by the module factory, plus resetting `captured` in a `finally`) addresses both halves.

Mechanically confirmed, and genuinely latent — I'd treat it as the lowest-priority item here. `packages/mochi/src/index.ts` has no `export default` (grep returns nothing), so `(realMod as {default?: unknown}).default` is `undefined` and L68 resolves `default` to the raw namespace object, whose `.Mochi` is the real class; only the explicit `Mochi:` key at L70 carries `mochiProxy`. I also confirmed the downstream premise rather than assuming it: `Mochi.serve` consults no build flag — a repo-wide grep shows `isBuildingEntry()` is read only by queue.ts (L934, L1024-1052, L1143) — so a `serve()` reached via the default binding really would bind a port mid-extraction, leaving `captured === null` and producing cli.ts L215's misleading 'No `routes` found' message (or, under the dev watcher, a bind against the port the live server holds). What caps this is the finding's own caveat, which I verified empirically: Bun 1.4.5 throws `SyntaxError: Missing 'default' export in module …` for a default import of a default-less ESM module, so an entry written as `import mochi from 'mochi-framework'` cannot boot under `bun run src/index.ts` at all. The only reachable manifestation is therefore `mochi-framework build` against an entry that is already invalid — a confusing error in place of the real SyntaxError — and nothing in the framework or the bundler emits a default import of the specifier (`format: 'esm'`/`target: 'bun'` preserves named imports; no CJS interop shim is in play). So: the defect is real and the docblock's stated invariant ('replacing `Mochi.serve` with a stub') is genuinely broken, but there is no scenario in which a working project is harmed. The one-line fix in the recommendation — build the exports object once and point `default` at the same proxied shape — is worth taking for the invariant alone.
